title: I’m building a trading platform that turns plain English into backtestable strategies — looking for beta testers
author: Upbeat-Caregiver8097
selftext:
​

Hey everyone,

I’ve been working on a trading platform that lets you describe a trading strategy in plain English and turn it into executable strategy code, without having to write everything manually.

It currently support 6-8 currency pairs and 5-7 commodities and 300+ crypto coins.

The interesting part is that it doesn’t just blindly convert your idea and run a backtest.

If something in your strategy is ambiguous or unclear, it asks follow-up questions to clarify your intended rules. Once the logic is clear, it generates visual evidence on a chart showing how the strategy interprets your idea. You can review the setup and verify whether it matches what you had in mind before running the backtest.

It also goes beyond basic RSI or moving-average strategies. It supports more advanced trading concepts, including:

\- Fair Value Gaps (FVGs)

\- Breakouts and other price-action setups

\- Fibonacci-based strategies

\- More complex combinations of trading conditions

\- Multi TF strategies 

For strategy validation, it includes:

\- Walk-forward testing

\- Bootstrap testing

\- Playbook testing

\- Performance metrics and a final pass/fail verdict

You can inspect the individual trades taken during a backtest, review the result of each trade, and examine chart-based evidence to understand why a trade was generated. The goal is to make the results more transparent instead of simply showing a profit percentage and expecting you to trust it.

Once a strategy is ready, you can deploy it for live signal generation and receive signals through Telegram. Risk management is built into the signal workflow: you configure your trading capital and risk settings, and the platform calculates a suggested position amount for each signal based on those settings.

There’s also a simple voice agent that lets you interact with and control supported platform workflows using voice commands.

I’m looking for a few crypto traders who would be willing to try the current build for free and give honest feedback.

I’m particularly interested in feedback from people who build or test their own strategies and know how frustrating it can be to translate an idea into precise rules and validate it properly.

This is a work in progress, and I’m not claiming that passing a backtest guarantees future profits. I want to find out where the workflow is useful, where it falls short, and what needs improvement.

And If you have any concerns and recommendations please share with me.

If you’re interested in testing it, leave a comment or send me a DM. Constructive criticism is welcome.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: asking back when a rule is ambiguous beats guessing. most of the bad backtests I've seen came from a converter quietly picking "close" when the person meant "touches it intraday".

replies.author: Upbeat-Caregiver8097
replies.body: That’s a solid point. Our system only asks clarification questions when a strategy rule is unclear, not every time. However, some strategies may require 8–10 questions. From a UX perspective, could this still frustrate users, and would you recommend any improvements to balance accuracy with a smooth user experience?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 8-10 in a row would lose people, yeah. ask only the ones that change the result, pick a default for the rest and show it in a plain summary, so someone fixes "close vs touches intraday" by editing one line instead of sitting through a quiz. that summary is also the thing they check before trusting the backtest.

replies.author: Upbeat-Caregiver8097
replies.body:

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's the hard version of the problem. when the video never says the stop, I'd show it as "not stated, we assumed X" in red next to the result, so nobody reads your backtest as the YouTuber's actual system. a blank you filled is still a guess.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Showing visual evidence of how the strategy was interpreted before running the backtest is a good safeguard, because wrong rule translation is a common hidden bug. For the validation side, I'd make sure the verdict shows how many variants the user tried in that session (since walk-forward and bootstrap don't remove selection from repeated re-runs), the trade count, and results with fees and funding included. The pass/fail should also be fixed before the run, with a clear rule, so it can't be tuned after seeing results. Crypto strategies often move around scheduled macro releases, and Cymetica's Crypto Outlook (simulated price-range scenarios for supported coins) is one way to stress-test ranges around them.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
Disclosure: I’m with QATS, which also works on strategy building and evaluation. One safeguard I would add is a versioned, machine-readable strategy specification between the plain-English input and every later action. It should show the exact instruments, timeframe, session and timezone, signal timing, order type, stop and target logic, sizing rule, fees, and every assumption the system supplied.



Give that specification an ID or hash and attach it to the backtest, each generated trade, and the live-signal process. Then a user can verify that the rules they approved are the rules that actually ran; a later parser or model change cannot silently alter an old strategy.



For beta testing, I would include contradictory prompts, missing stop logic, unavailable historical fields, daylight-saving changes, and two identical prompts submitted twice. A deterministic result or an explicit “cannot determine” state is safer than a plausible interpretation that changes between runs.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
Interesting project. The visual verification before running a backtest is a good idea.

One failure case I'd specifically test is multi-timeframe lookahead.

For example, a strategy might use a 5-minute entry signal combined with confirmation from a 1-hour candle.

The generated chart can look perfectly reasonable while the backtest accidentally uses information from the hourly candle before that candle has actually closed.

I'd test the generated strategy through a strictly chronological replay and verify that every decision uses only information available at that exact timestamp.

I'm building TIYlab, a non-custodial Bitcoin portfolio automation system, and distinguishing strategy logic from the evidence used to validate it is something I consider particularly important.

I'd also be careful with the final pass/fail verdict. Passing walk-forward and bootstrap tests doesn't necessarily establish a genuine trading edge, especially after repeated revisions.

Does your engine explicitly track when each input becomes available, rather than just the timestamp of the candle it belongs to?
